sections.title: Recognizing the species
sections.text: Tricholoma columbetta is a white tricholoma with a silky, fibrillose cap, sometimes cream at the centre; it begins convex and later flattens, and may be slightly sticky when young or damp. The white gills are crowded and emarginate near the stem; their edges may become irregular and pink-stained. The stem is white, fibrillose and sometimes rooting.

sections.title: Stem base and useful characters
sections.text: The stem base may show blue, green or pink staining, although this is not always present. The firm flesh is white, with a farinaceous smell and a mild or slightly farinaceous taste. The spore print is white. The stem has neither ring nor volva, but the entire base must be checked because a volva may be buried.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: It grows singly or in small groups on soil in broad-leaved woodland, especially with oak, beech or birch, usually on acid to neutral soils; it is less common under conifers. It fruits from summer to autumn, with exact timing depending on local climate.

sections.title: Lookalikes and safety
sections.text: Deadly white Amanita species, including Amanita virosa and the white forms of A. phalloides or A. verna, can be confused with white tricholomas. The volva may remain underground and a ring may be missing, damaged or hidden; neither character alone makes an identification safe. Entoloma sinuatum has pale gills when young that turn pink at maturity. Lyon 1, DGfM and VAPKO list this species as edible; have any collection checked by a qualified person.

traits: White silky, fibrillose cap, sometimes cream at the centre, convex then flattened; slightly sticky when young or damp
Crowded, emarginate white gills, sometimes pink-stained, with an edge that may become irregular
White fibrillose stem, sometimes rooting; base may stain blue, green or pink
Firm white flesh, farinaceous smell, mild to slightly farinaceous taste; white spore print
Broad-leaved woodland, especially oak, beech and birch, on acid to neutral soils · summer and autumn
Listed as edible by mycological sources; can be confused with deadly white Amanitas
safetyNote: Listed as edible by Lyon 1, DGfM and VAPKO, but deadly white Amanitas can look similar. A buried volva or a missing ring can escape notice; never eat a collection identified only from a photo or entry, and have it checked by a qualified person.
